facts.claim: "Baby's on Fire" is the third track on Brian Eno's debut solo album Here Come the Warm Jets. Wikipedia dates the album to 1974, while other sources say 1973.
Eno wrote and produced the song, and he handled production and mixing for most of the album.
The track was recorded in September 1973 at Majestic Studios in Clapham, London. Eno had recorded most of his earlier material there.
The musicians credited on the track are Simon King, Marty Simon, Robert Fripp, Paul Rudolph and John Wetton, plus Eno himself.
Eno is credited with vocals and synthesizer, John Wetton with bass, and Paul Rudolph with guitar. Robert Fripp's long guitar solo dominates the recording.
Fripp's solo runs about three minutes over shifting drum accents. It continues through the return of Eno's vocals without following the beat.
Fripp said he played the solo right after getting off a plane from America, and that he was exhausted.

Eno said the song starts out sounding very sinister but has very ordinary words, sung with an incredible amount of passion. He also said he chooses words for their vowel sounds and aggression rather than meaning, and joked that it could have been "Baby's on hire".
The song is a surreal fantasy about a photography session involving a burning woman, unthinking laughing onlookers, and two second-hand tobacconists.

Eno wrote "Baby's on Fire" right after leaving Roxy Music, and one writer calls it bitterly cynical. Most of the rest of the album's lyrics were improvised in response to the recorded instrumental tracks.

research.lineage: The song belongs to Eno's early-to-mid-1970s experimental pop and art-rock phase after he left glam and art-rock band Roxy Music. This came before his turn to ambient music, and AllMusic describes those albums as bridging the two styles.

draft:
"Take your time she's only burning." A photographer's instruction, said as calmly as a note about lighting, and it's the coldest line in **Baby's On Fire**. Brian Eno builds the song around a woman in flames and a crowd that treats her as a subject. Laughing boys wait for photos. Rescuers are told to talk about something else. The wind is asked to help the fire along. Nobody reaches for her. The cruelty isn't the fire itself. It's how ordinary everyone stays around it.

Eno once said the song starts out sounding sinister but uses very ordinary words, sung with an incredible amount of passion. He said he picks words for their vowels and their aggression more than their meaning, and joked it could just as well have been "Baby's on hire." Even taken at his word, the attitude comes through in the sound of the words. Nursery-rhyme doubling falls on the rowers, the wind and the clicking shutters, playground chants for a scene of someone being hurt. Then comes the surreal detour to Juanita and Juan, second-hand tobacco sellers who pocket whatever is left in the ashtrays. It widens the frame to a world where everyone is scavenging something.

He wrote it right after leaving Roxy Music, and one writer has called it bitterly cynical. The narrator's own wound flickers through in "I could be half the man I used to," a line that cuts off before its last word. Spite and self-pity share that line, and the song doesn't sort them out. The final verse shrugs at the whole spectacle: "But any idiot would know that."

The band plays it straight, which is what makes it unnerving. A drum kit drives a steady beat with the snare out front. John Wetton's bass repeats a simple line. A distorted guitar holds sustained chords while a high synth pad shimmers overhead. The room sounds raw and a little distant. Eno's voice is clear, slightly nasal and detached, with no harmonies to soften it. The track was recorded in September 1973 at Majestic Studios in Clapham, with Paul Rudolph on guitar and Simon King and Marty Simon also credited. It belongs to Eno's art-rock and experimental pop stretch between Roxy Music and the ambient records.

Then there's Robert Fripp. His solo runs about three minutes over shifting drum accents and keeps going straight through Eno's return to the mic, refusing to follow the beat. Fripp said he played it fresh off a plane from America, exhausted. Surrounded by bystanders who can't be bothered, the one player who won't fall in line ends up as the song's only real disturbance.

The groove makes you one of the onlookers, nodding along while someone burns, and the small guilt of enjoying it is exactly what keeps pulling you back.
